He remains the technical architect behind Mistral's model line, from the first 7B release through its largest frontier models.
people.name: Guillaume Lample
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Scientist, Mistral AI

people.hook: Hans Moravec was born in Kautzen, Austria, in 1948 and moved to Canada as a child, earning a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Acadia University in 1969 and a master's in computer science from the University of Western Ontario in 1971. He completed a Ph.D. in computer science at Stanford University in 1980, building an early mobile robot that used a television camera and an onboard computer to navigate cluttered rooms. He then joined Carnegie Mellon University, where he directed the Mobile Robot Laboratory at the Robotics Institute for twenty-five years, developing three-dimensional occupancy grid mapping that let robots build spatial maps from noisy sensor data. In his 1988 book Mind Children, he observed that tasks requiring abstract reasoning are computationally easy for machines while tasks requiring basic sensorimotor skills, such as walking or recognizing a face, are extremely hard, an observation now known as Moravec's paradox. In 2003 he co-founded Seegrid Corporation to commercialize automated guided vehicle technology built on his mapping research, serving as its chief scientist.
people.name: Hans Moravec
people.moniker: Roboticist known for Moravec's paradox

people.hook: Helen Toner is executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, where she studies the security implications of AI, export controls, and US-China technology competition. Born and raised in Australia, she holds a BSc in chemical engineering from the University of Melbourne before moving into technology policy, first as a senior research analyst at Open Philanthropy advising on AI grantmaking, then as a research affiliate at Oxford's Centre for the Governance of AI, spending nine months in Beijing studying China's AI ecosystem. In September 2021 she joined OpenAI's board of directors. She left the board in November 2023, after the board's brief removal and reinstatement of CEO Sam Altman, a crisis in which she said the board had been kept in the dark about matters including the launch of ChatGPT and Altman's ownership stake in the OpenAI Startup Fund. She has since testified before multiple congressional committees on AI policy and continues to lead CSET's research program.
people.name: Helen Toner
people.moniker: Executive director, Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology

people.hook: Herbert Simon entered the University of Chicago in 1933 hoping to become what he called a mathematical social scientist, studying under mentors including the logician Rudolf Carnap and political scientist Charles Merriam. After finishing his undergraduate degree in 1936 and later a PhD, he built a career studying how organizations and individuals actually make decisions under limits of time, knowledge and computing power, a theory he called bounded rationality. In 1949 he joined the Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University, to help build its Graduate School of Industrial Administration around economics and behavioral science. Around 1954 he began working with Allen Newell to use computer simulation to study human problem solving, and together with Cliff Shaw they built the Logic Theorist in 1956, widely considered the first program designed to mimic human reasoning, followed by the more general General Problem Solver in 1957. Simon spent the rest of his career at Carnegie Mellon studying cognition, organizations and artificial intelligence, work recognized with the 1975 ACM Turing Award, shared with Newell, and the 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his research on decision making in economic organizations.
people.name: Herbert Simon
people.moniker: Nobel laureate who founded artificial intelligence alongside Allen Newell

people.hook: Hubert Dreyfus was born in Terre Haute, Indiana, in 1929 and studied philosophy at Harvard, earning his doctorate in 1964. While teaching at MIT in the early 1960s, he was asked by the RAND Corporation to evaluate the prospects of artificial intelligence and concluded, against the confident predictions of the field's founders, that AI's symbolic, rule-based approach could not capture the embodied, skillful coping that underlies everyday human intelligence. He expanded this critique into the 1972 book What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason, drawing on the phenomenology of Martin Heidegger and Maurice Merleau-Ponty to argue that meaning and skill arise from a body acting in a world, not from symbols manipulated in a mind. He moved to the University of California, Berkeley, in 1968, where he taught for the rest of his career and became one of the most influential interpreters of Heidegger in America. He updated his argument in What Computers Still Can't Do (1992) as the field shifted toward neural networks, and his claim that intelligence depends on a body skillfully coping with a world anticipated the embodied and situated approaches that later reshaped robotics and AI.
people.name: Hubert Dreyfus
people.moniker: Philosopher who challenged AI with phenomenology

people.hook: Hugo Touvron holds two bachelor's degrees, from Ecole Polytechnique and Paris Dauphine University, and three master's degrees in mathematics and computer science from Ecole Polytechnique, ENS Paris-Saclay, and ENSTA ParisTech. He joined Facebook AI Research in November 2019 as a resident PhD student advised by Herve Jegou at Facebook and Matthieu Cord at Sorbonne University, where his early work centered on data-efficient image transformers and vision transfer learning, including the DeiT and DeiT III papers. He then moved into large language models, becoming lead author of LLaMA, Meta's open-weights foundation language model released in February 2023, followed by Llama 2 in July 2023 and a contribution to Code Llama in August 2023. His work helped establish the open-weights LLaMA family as a widely used alternative to closed frontier models.
people.name: Hugo Touvron
people.moniker: Research Scientist, Meta AI (FAIR)

people.hook: Ian Goodfellow studied computer science at Stanford University, earning undergraduate and masters degrees while working with Andrew Ng, before completing a PhD in machine learning at the Universite de Montreal in 2015 under Yoshua Bengio and Aaron Courville. While a graduate student he devised Generative Adversarial Networks, a framework in which two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, are trained against each other so the generator learns to produce increasingly realistic data. He and his coauthors described the idea in a 2014 paper that became one of the most influential works in deep learning and gave rise to a large body of research on image synthesis and generative modeling. After completing his PhD he continued this line of research at OpenAI, contributing to work on improving the stability of GAN training. He also co-authored the widely used textbook Deep Learning with Bengio and Courville, published by MIT Press in 2016.
people.name: Ian Goodfellow
people.moniker: Inventor of Generative Adversarial Networks

people.hook: Ian T. Jolliffe is a British statistician who completed his PhD at the University of Sussex before building his academic career at the University of Aberdeen, where he became a professor of statistics. He worked extensively on principal component analysis, a method for reducing the number of variables in a dataset while preserving as much of its variability as possible. In 1986 he published the first edition of his textbook Principal Component Analysis, which organized and extended the scattered literature on the technique into a single reference. A substantially expanded second edition followed in 2002, nearly doubling the material and adding coverage of newer variants and applications. His textbook became the standard reference work for the method across statistics, and PCA itself became one of the most widely used tools for dimensionality reduction in modern data analysis and machine learning. He is also a member of the American Statistical Association.
people.name: Ian T. Jolliffe
people.moniker: Statistician who formalized Principal Component Analysis

people.hook: Illia Polosukhin worked as a machine learning engineer at Google, where he contributed to high level APIs for TensorFlow and worked on question answering systems used in Google Search. In 2017 he was one of eight coauthors of the paper Attention Is All You Need, which introduced the Transformer architecture built entirely on attention mechanisms and became the foundation for the large language models that followed. The next year he left Google and, together with Alexander Skidanov and other collaborators, began building a new blockchain protocol out of a small office in San Francisco. That project became NEAR Protocol, a sharded, proof of stake blockchain designed for usability and scalability, which launched its mainnet in 2020. Polosukhin continues to serve as a co-founder of NEAR, and has more recently worked on bringing large language model and AI agent technology into the NEAR ecosystem.
people.name: Illia Polosukhin
people.moniker: Co-founder, NEAR Protocol

people.hook: Ilya Sutskever was born in Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, and moved with his family first to Israel and then to Canada, where he studied computer science at the University of Toronto under Geoffrey Hinton. In 2012 he co-authored the AlexNet paper with Alex Krizhevsky and Hinton, a deep convolutional network that sharply cut ImageNet classification error rates and helped launch the modern deep learning era. He followed this in 2014 with Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks, showing that a general encoder-decoder architecture could handle tasks like machine translation. In December 2015 he co-founded OpenAI, serving first as Research Director and later as Chief Scientist while the lab built its GPT model series. He left OpenAI in 2024 and co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc with Daniel Gross and Daniel Levy, a company dedicated to a single goal, building safe superintelligence, and became its CEO in mid-2025 after Gross departed.
people.name: Ilya Sutskever
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Safe Superintelligence Inc.

people.hook: Suh spent over 23 years at IBM, rising to head global strategic partnerships worth more than $10 billion before leading Watson AI product units in commerce, supply chain and collaboration; she then served as President of DocuSign and on its board through its 2018 IPO before becoming CEO of Niantic Spatial, a company building real-world foundation models for physical AI.
people.name: Inhi Cho Suh
people.moniker: CEO, Niantic Spatial

people.hook: Ion Stoica earned his PhD in computer science at Carnegie Mellon University before joining the UC Berkeley faculty in 2001, where he has remained a professor of electrical engineering and computer sciences ever since. His research group at Berkeley, first AMPLab and later RISELab, became a pipeline for widely used open source infrastructure and startups. He co-founded the video analytics company Conviva in 2006, then co-created Apache Mesos, an early cluster resource manager, before helping commercialize Apache Spark by co-founding Databricks in 2013. Working with graduate students including Robert Nishihara and Philipp Moritz, he later co-created Ray, a distributed execution framework for scaling Python and machine learning workloads, and co-founded Anyscale in 2019 to build a company around it. He continues to teach and direct systems research at Berkeley while serving in leadership roles at both companies.
people.name: Ion Stoica
people.moniker: Co-founder of Databricks and Anyscale, UC Berkeley professor

people.hook: Ivan Zhang studied computer science at the University of Toronto, graduating in 2016, and worked as an engineer across biotech and MLOps roles before co-founding the research collective for.ai in 2017. In 2019 he co-founded Cohere alongside Aidan Gomez and Nick Frosst, building the company into an enterprise-focused large language model provider. As co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Zhang has overseen technical product development at Cohere and worked closely with the company's public sector and government customers. For.ai, the research group he started before Cohere, was later folded into Cohere as its open research division, Cohere Labs. He has co-authored research spanning generative adversarial networks, model regularization and AI safety.
people.name: Ivan Zhang
people.moniker: Co-founder and CTO of Cohere

people.hook: J.C.R. Licklider trained as an experimental psychologist, earning his PhD at the University of Rochester before working on psychoacoustics at Harvard during the Second World War. He later moved into engineering circles at MIT, where hands-on exposure to early computers convinced him that machines could become active partners in human thought rather than passive calculators. In 1957 he ran a self study tracking his own workday and found that most of his time went to mechanical tasks that stood between him and actual thinking, an observation that fed directly into his influential 1960 paper Man-Computer Symbiosis, which argued that people and computers should work together in close, real time partnership. In 1962 he became the first director of the Information Processing Techniques Office at the Advanced Research Projects Agency, where he funded university computer science research across the country and, in an internal 1963 memo, sketched an early vision of computers linked together into what he called an intergalactic network. That funding program and the community of researchers it supported helped lay the intellectual groundwork that led to the ARPANET later in the decade.
people.name: J.C.R. Licklider
people.moniker: Psychologist who envisioned human-computer symbiosis and funded the roots of the internet

people.hook: Jack Clark is a co-founder of Anthropic who began his career as a technical journalist covering distributed systems, quantum computing and AI for Bloomberg Businessweek and The Register. In September 2016 he joined OpenAI, where he became policy director and helped build the organization's early approach to AI policy. In 2017 he became a founding member of Stanford's AI Index, the annual report that tracks the state of global AI progress, and later served as an inaugural member of the US National AI Advisory Committee. In 2021 he co-founded Anthropic and led its policy work as co-founder and head of policy, while continuing to publish Import AI, a weekly newsletter on AI research and policy now read by more than 100,000 subscribers. He has testified before Congress on the importance of democratic countries leading AI development. In March 2026, he moved into a new role as Anthropic's Head of Public Benefit, leading the newly formed Anthropic Institute, a research effort on AI's societal, economic and legal impact.
people.name: Jack Clark
people.moniker: Co-founder of Anthropic, head of the Anthropic Institute

people.hook: Mineart began as a mechanical engineer at Caterpillar in 1999 and spent nearly three decades rising through engineering, product strategy, and electric power leadership roles before being named Chief Technology Officer, now leading Cat Technology's push to integrate smarter, more connected machines across Caterpillar's global equipment lines.
people.name: Jaime Mineart
people.moniker: Chief Technology Officer of Caterpillar

people.hook: Jakob Uszkoreit grew up in Saarbrücken, Germany, and studied computer science and mathematics at the Berlin Institute of Technology, completing his master's degree summa cum laude in 2008. He joined Google that year after an earlier research internship, working first on data mining for Google Translate and later leading a semantic parsing team supporting Google Search and Assistant. In 2017 he co-authored Attention Is All You Need with colleagues at Google Brain, introducing the Transformer architecture that replaced recurrence and convolution with self-attention and became the foundation for most large language models built since. In 2021 he left Google to co-found Inceptive with biochemist Rhiju Das, applying deep learning models to the design of RNA-based medicines and pairing computational predictions with laboratory testing.
people.name: Jakob Uszkoreit
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Inceptive

people.hook: Jakub Pachocki joined OpenAI in 2017 as a theoretical computer scientist fresh from a PhD in convex optimization, and rose to run the research programs behind some of the company's largest bets, including GPT-4 and the reinforcement-learning system that beat the world Dota 2 champions. In May 2024 OpenAI named him Chief Scientist, succeeding Ilya Sutskever, putting him in charge of the company's core research direction. He is credited with helping steer OpenAI toward reasoning models that work through problems step by step, an approach that produced systems scoring at gold-medal level on the International Mathematical Olympiad. Sam Altman has called him one of the strongest research minds at the company.
people.name: Jakub Pachocki
people.moniker: Chief Scientist, OpenAI

people.hook: Jared Kaplan built his early career as a theoretical physicist, holding a PhD from Harvard and a faculty position at Johns Hopkins studying quantum gravity and conformal field theory. Starting in 2018 he turned that background toward machine learning, working on how language model performance scales with compute, data and parameters, research his own university describes as feeding into GPT-3. In 2021 he co-founded Anthropic and became its Chief Science Officer, leading the technical research behind models like Claude and methods such as Constitutional AI. He still holds his Johns Hopkins physics appointment alongside his role at Anthropic.
people.name: Jared Kaplan
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Science Officer, Anthropic

people.hook: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein worked across physics and neuroscience, including pre-doctoral work related to NASA Mars rover research, before turning fully to machine learning. He earned his PhD in 2012 at the Redwood Center for Theoretical Neuroscience at UC Berkeley, studying under Bruno Olshausen. While a visiting scholar in Surya Ganguli's lab at Stanford, he led the 2015 paper Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics, which showed how to learn a generative model by reversing a slow diffusion process that gradually destroys the structure of training data. The technique laid the mathematical groundwork later built on by denoising diffusion probabilistic models, which became the basis for modern image generation systems. He then worked as a research scientist and later principal scientist at Google Brain and Google DeepMind, studying the theory of large neural networks, learned optimizers, and the capabilities of large language models, before joining Anthropic as a member of technical staff.
people.name: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein
people.moniker: Pioneer of diffusion based generative models

people.hook: Jason Weston earned his PhD in machine learning in 2000 from Royal Holloway, University of London, completing his doctoral research at AT&T Research in Red Bank, New Jersey under Alex Gammerman, Volodya Vovk and Vladimir Vapnik. He then worked as a researcher at Biowulf Technologies before moving to the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Tubingen and later NEC Labs America. In 2009 he joined Google as a research scientist in New York, and in 2014 he moved to Facebook AI Research, now Meta AI, where he has continued as a research scientist while also serving as a visiting research professor at NYU. That same year he introduced memory networks with Sumit Chopra and Antoine Bordes, a class of models that pair a neural network with an explicit, addressable memory component so a system can read and write facts needed to answer questions or hold a conversation over a long context. He also helped design the bAbI benchmark suite, giving researchers a controlled way to test whether models could handle reasoning tasks such as multi step inference and coreference.
people.name: Jason Weston
people.moniker: Pioneer of memory augmented neural networks

people.hook: Patel has run product at four different points along enterprise software's evolution, content management at Doculabs, cloud file sync at EMC and Syncplicity, cloud content at Box, and now security, collaboration, and AI infrastructure at Cisco, rising to President and Chief Product Officer as the company repositions its networking core around AI.
people.name: Jeetu Patel
people.moniker: President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco

people.hook: Jeff Dean earned a bachelor's degree in computer science and economics from the University of Minnesota in 1990 and a PhD in computer science from the University of Washington in 1996, then worked at Digital Equipment Corporation before joining Google in 1999. At Google he co-designed MapReduce with Sanjay Ghemawat in 2004 and Bigtable in 2006, two systems that became core infrastructure for processing and storing data at massive scale. In 2011 he co-founded the Google Brain team, and in 2015 he helped design and open source TensorFlow, one of the most widely used machine learning frameworks. He also pushed Google to build custom AI accelerator chips, leading to multiple generations of Tensor Processing Units, and now serves as Chief Scientist for Google Research and Google DeepMind, helping set the company's AI research direction.
people.name: Jeff Dean
people.moniker: Chief Scientist, Google Research and Google DeepMind

people.hook: Jensen Huang founded NVIDIA in 1993 and has run it continuously ever since, first as a graphics chip maker for PC gaming and later as the dominant supplier of the GPUs that power modern AI training and inference. He holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Oregon State University and a master's from Stanford, and worked at LSI Logic and Advanced Micro Devices before starting NVIDIA. Under his leadership the company introduced the GPU in 1999, a product line that eventually became the core infrastructure of the generative AI boom. He has since been recognized with engineering's biggest honors, including a share of the 2025 Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering and the 2026 IEEE Medal of Honor.
people.name: Jensen Huang
people.moniker: Founder, President and CEO, NVIDIA

people.hook: Jerome Friedman trained as a physicist, earning a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley before working as a research physicist in high-energy physics. In 1972 he joined the Stanford Computation Research Group, and in 1982 he was appointed a professor of statistics at Stanford University. With Leo Breiman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees (CART), published in 1984, and in 1991 he introduced Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) in the Annals of Statistics. In 2001 he published Greedy Function Approximation, formalizing gradient boosting machines as a general method that later became central to widely used tools for structured data prediction. He also co-authored the textbook The Elements of Statistical Learning with Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, and is now Professor of Statistics, Emeritus, at Stanford.
people.name: Jerome Friedman
people.moniker: Professor of Statistics, Emeritus, Stanford University

people.hook: Jian Sun was born in Xi'an, China, in 1977 and earned his bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees, all from Xi'an Jiaotong University, completing his PhD in 2003. He then spent thirteen years at Microsoft Research Asia working on computer vision and computer graphics, contributing to technologies including Windows Hello facial recognition, Kinect Identity, and the Computer Vision and Face APIs for Microsoft Azure. In 2015, with Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang and Shaoqing Ren, he co-authored Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition, which introduced residual connections that let neural networks be trained far deeper than before by having layers learn a difference from their input rather than a full transformation. The resulting ResNet architecture won the ImageNet and COCO competitions in 2015 and became one of the most widely used building blocks in computer vision. In July 2016 he joined Megvii, the Beijing based computer vision company behind Face++, as Chief Scientist and Managing Director of Research, and from January 2019 he also served as Dean of the College of Artificial Intelligence at Xi'an Jiaotong University. He died on June 14, 2022.
people.name: Jian Sun
people.moniker: Co-creator of ResNet, former Megvii chief scientist

people.hook: Fowler ran technology for one of America's largest industrial conglomerates, GE, where he oversaw a $3 billion budget and 25,000 employees and drove the insourcing of thousands of technology jobs, before leading Nationwide's digital transformation and now shaping Lumen's AI-driven network strategy as its CTPO.
people.name: Jim Fowler
people.moniker: Chief Technology and Product Officer at Lumen Technologies

people.hook: Jim Keller has spent four decades moving between the biggest names in semiconductors, leaving a distinct architecture behind at each stop. He led design of AMD's Zen microarchitecture, the chip line credited with reviving the company's competitiveness against Intel, and earlier led the engineering behind Apple's A4 and A5 mobile processors after Apple acquired P.A. Semi. He later ran Autopilot hardware engineering at Tesla and Silicon Engineering at Intel before moving into AI accelerator chips. He is now CEO of Tenstorrent and has also co-founded Atomic Semi, a startup building small-scale chip fabs.
people.name: Jim Keller
people.moniker: CEO, Tenstorrent

people.hook: Jimmy Ba completed his undergraduate degree at the University of Toronto in 2011 and his master's degree there in 2014, studying under Brendan Frey and Ruslan Salakhutdinov, before finishing his PhD under Geoffrey Hinton. In 2014 he co-authored Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization with Diederik Kingma, introducing an optimization algorithm that combines adaptive learning rates with momentum and became the default choice for training most deep learning models. In 2016 he co-authored Layer Normalization with Jamie Ryan Kiros and Geoffrey Hinton, a technique that normalizes the inputs to each layer of a network across its features rather than across a batch, making it effective for recurrent networks and later a standard component of Transformer architectures. He became an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto, where he holds a CIFAR AI Chair and is affiliated with the Vector Institute. His research has continued to focus on efficient learning algorithms for deep neural networks, spanning reinforcement learning and natural language processing.
people.name: Jimmy Ba
people.moniker: Co-inventor of the Adam optimizer and Layer Normalization

people.hook: Jitendra Malik was born in 1960 and earned his undergraduate degree at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur before completing his PhD at Stanford University. He joined the faculty of the University of California, Berkeley, where he became the Arthur J. Chick Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences. With his student Jianbo Shi, he developed the normalized cuts algorithm, a graph based method for image segmentation published in 2000 that treated grouping pixels into regions as a graph partitioning problem and became one of the most cited techniques in computer vision. His research group's later work, including the region proposal based R-CNN approach to object detection developed with his students, helped connect classical computer vision with the deep learning era. Over his career at Berkeley he has supervised more than 40 PhD students and numerous postdoctoral researchers who have gone on to research and leadership roles at companies and universities including Google, Meta, MIT and Carnegie Mellon.
people.name: Jitendra Malik
people.moniker: Pioneer of computer vision and image segmentation

people.hook: John Hopfield was born in Chicago, Illinois, in 1933 and earned his Ph.D. in physics from Cornell University in 1958. He worked at Bell Labs and held professorships in physics at Princeton, in chemistry and biology at Caltech, and later in molecular biology back at Princeton, moving between physics and biology throughout his career. In 1982 he published Neural Networks and Physical Systems with Emergent Collective Computational Abilities, describing a network of simple, interconnected units that settles into stable patterns the way a physical system settles toward low energy, and showing that such a network can store and recall memories from partial or noisy input. The design, now called the Hopfield network, gave neural network research a rigorous physical and mathematical footing at a time when the field had lost much of its funding and credibility, and it became a foundation for later work in associative memory, optimization, and machine learning. In 2024 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Geoffrey Hinton for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks.
people.name: John Hopfield
people.moniker: Physicist who invented the Hopfield network

people.hook: John McCarthy earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Caltech in 1948 and a PhD in mathematics from Princeton in 1951. In August 1955, together with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, he wrote the proposal for a summer research project at Dartmouth College built on the idea that every aspect of learning or intelligence could in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it, a document that introduced the field's name. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop that followed brought together many of the researchers who would go on to define artificial intelligence as a discipline. While at MIT in 1958, McCarthy created the Lisp programming language, which became the dominant tool for AI research for decades because of its ability to manipulate symbolic expressions. He moved to Stanford University in 1962, where he founded the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and continued developing logic based approaches to reasoning and knowledge representation until his retirement in 2000.
people.name: John McCarthy
people.moniker: Coined the term artificial intelligence and created the Lisp programming language

people.hook: John Searle was born in Denver, Colorado, in 1932 and studied philosophy at the University of Wisconsin before winning a Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford, where he earned his doctorate under J. L. Austin and P. F. Strawson. He joined the philosophy department at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1959 and remained there for the rest of his career, becoming the Slusser Professor of Philosophy of Mind and Language. Building on his early work in speech act theory, he published Minds, Brains, and Programs in 1980, introducing the Chinese Room thought experiment: a person who manipulates Chinese symbols by following an English rulebook can produce correct answers without understanding a word of Chinese, which Searle argued shows that running the right program is not sufficient for genuine understanding. The argument became one of the most debated texts in philosophy of mind and cognitive science, directly challenging the claim that a sufficiently sophisticated computer program could think. He continued to develop the argument and its implications for consciousness across decades of subsequent books, including The Rediscovery of the Mind (1992), and remained an active commentator on AI and machine understanding into the era of large language models.
people.name: John Searle
people.moniker: Philosopher who devised the Chinese Room argument

people.hook: Whyte became CEO of the American Medical Association in 2025 after nearly seven years as Chief Medical Officer of WebMD, and earlier spent nearly five years at the FDA and over eight years as chief medical expert at Discovery Channel. He holds an MD and an MPH from Harvard.
people.name: John Whyte
people.moniker: CEO, American Medical Association

people.hook: John von Neumann was born on December 28, 1903, in Budapest, Hungary, and earned a doctorate in mathematics from Pazmany Peter University in 1926 while also training as a chemical engineer in Zurich. He emigrated to the United States in 1930 and in 1933 became one of the founding professors of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, working alongside Albert Einstein and Kurt Godel. During and after World War II he contributed to the Manhattan Project and to early computing efforts, and in 1945 he wrote the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, which described a computer that stores its program and data together in the same memory. That stored-program design, since called the von Neumann architecture, became the basis for the IAS machine he built at Princeton and for nearly all computers that followed. He continued advising the United States government on computing and nuclear policy until his death from cancer on February 8, 1957, in Washington, D.C.
people.name: John von Neumann
people.moniker: Mathematician who defined modern computer architecture

people.hook: Jonathan Ho earned his PhD in electrical engineering and computer science at UC Berkeley, advised by Pieter Abbeel, working on generative models including GANs and normalizing flows. In 2020 he wrote Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models as lead author, a paper that showed diffusion based generative models could match the image quality of GANs. The DDPM formulation became the technical backbone behind Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2 and Imagen. He later joined Google Research, where he co-authored Imagen and Video Diffusion Models, and in 2022 published Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance, a technique now standard in nearly every production text-to-image system.
people.name: Jonathan Ho
people.moniker: Lead author of the DDPM diffusion model paper

people.hook: Jonathan Ross started what became Google's Tensor Processing Unit as an internal side project, then left to found Groq in 2016, building a chip architecture designed purely for AI inference. Groq's language processing units made the company one of the most closely watched hardware challengers to Nvidia. In December 2025 Nvidia took a non-exclusive license to Groq's technology and hired Ross along with most of Groq's engineering team, a deal that returned billions of dollars to Groq's shareholders and moved its founder inside the company his chips were built to compete with. Ross now works at Nvidia as its chief software architect, and has spoken candidly about the leadership mistakes he made running Groq for nearly a decade.
people.name: Jonathan Ross
people.moniker: Chief Software Architect at Nvidia, founder of Groq

people.hook: Reis-Filho built his career deciphering cancer genomics at the bench, at the Institute of Cancer Research and then as Chief of Experimental Pathology at Memorial Sloan Kettering, before moving to AstraZeneca to apply AI foundation models and agentic frameworks directly to drug discovery and clinical development, one of the clearer examples of a working oncologist becoming an enterprise AI leader.
people.name: Jorge Reis-Filho
people.moniker: Chief of AI for Science Innovation at AstraZeneca

people.hook: Joseph Weizenbaum was born on January 8, 1923, in Berlin, Germany, and fled with his family to the United States in the 1930s as the Nazi regime tightened its persecution of Jews. He studied mathematics at Wayne University in Detroit, worked on early digital computers there, and later helped design the ERMA banking computer system at General Electric in the 1950s. In 1963 he joined the faculty of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and in 1966 he published ELIZA, a program that used simple pattern matching to imitate a psychotherapist's responses, in a paper for Communications of the ACM. Weizenbaum was troubled that people, including his own secretary, treated ELIZA's replies as though they carried real understanding, and the experience turned him into one of computing's most prominent internal critics. In his 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason he argued that some human judgments should never be delegated to a machine, a position he held until his death on March 5, 2008, in Berlin.
people.name: Joseph Weizenbaum
people.moniker: Computer scientist who created ELIZA

people.hook: Joy Buolamwini is a computer scientist whose research exposed how commercial facial recognition systems perform far worse on darker skinned faces than lighter skinned ones. While a graduate researcher at the MIT Media Lab, she found that some facial analysis software failed to detect her own face until she put on a white mask, an experience that led her to start systematically testing commercial systems for bias. In 2016 she founded the Algorithmic Justice League to combine research, art, and advocacy against harmful bias in AI systems. Her 2018 study Gender Shades, co-authored with Timnit Gebru, tested facial analysis products from IBM, Microsoft, and Face++ using a new benchmark built from images of parliamentarians in African and European countries, and found error rates for darker skinned women far higher than for lighter skinned men. She holds a bachelor's degree in computer science from the Georgia Institute of Technology, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and earned her PhD from the MIT Media Lab. Her work has since informed congressional testimony on facial recognition technology, the 2020 documentary Coded Bias, and her 2023 book Unmasking AI.
people.name: Joy Buolamwini
people.moniker: Computer scientist and founder of the Algorithmic Justice League

people.hook: Judea Pearl earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the Technion in Israel in 1960, then went on to complete master's degrees in electronics and physics in the United States before earning a PhD in electrical engineering from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn in 1965. He joined the computer science faculty at UCLA in 1969 and later founded its Cognitive Systems Laboratory. In the 1980s Pearl developed Bayesian networks, a mathematical framework for representing and reasoning about uncertain relationships among many variables, set out in his 1988 monograph Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems, which reshaped how artificial intelligence systems handle uncertainty. He then turned to an even harder problem, building a formal calculus, including what he called the do-calculus, for distinguishing genuine causation from mere correlation using data, work collected in his 2000 book Causality. He later explained these ideas for a general audience in The Book of Why, published in 2018. For this body of work he received the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 2011.
people.name: Judea Pearl
people.moniker: Creator of Bayesian networks and the modern mathematics of causal reasoning

people.hook: Julian Schrittwieser is an Austrian software engineer and AI researcher. He worked at Google DeepMind for years, where he was a key contributor to AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero and the lead author of MuZero, a reinforcement learning algorithm that mastered Go, chess, shogi, and Atari games while learning its own model of each game's rules. He went on to work on AlphaTensor, AlphaDev, and AlphaCode, and later on AlphaProof, which reached silver-medal-level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. In 2025 he moved to Anthropic to continue AI research. He also writes a technical blog, at julian.ac, about AI progress and software engineering.
people.name: Julian Schrittwieser
people.moniker: AI researcher, co-creator of MuZero

people.hook: Julien Chaumond co-founded Hugging Face in 2016 and has served as its chief technology officer since, building the technical infrastructure, the Hub, the Transformers library, and the huggingface_hub client, that turned the company into the default distribution point for open machine learning models. Before Hugging Face he ran two earlier startups, Prodcast and the reading platform Glose, and advised the French Deputy Minister for Digital Affairs. He describes Hugging Face's approach as belonging to its user community rather than standing apart from it, a framing that has shaped the company's open-source strategy as its Hub scaled to millions of hosted models and datasets.
people.name: Julien Chaumond
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Hugging Face

people.hook: Jürgen Schmidhuber was born in Munich, Germany, and earned his doctorate in computer science from the Technical University of Munich in 1991. In 1990 he proposed an early adversarial training scheme in which two neural networks competed against each other, an idea later recognized as anticipating generative adversarial networks. In 1997 he and his student Sepp Hochreiter published Long Short-Term Memory, a recurrent neural network architecture that overcame the vanishing gradient problem and became one of the most widely used designs in speech recognition and language modeling before the rise of Transformers. He has long served as Scientific Director of the Swiss AI Lab IDSIA, and since 2021 has also directed the AI Initiative at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology. He co-founded NNAISENSE, a company applying his lab's neural network research to industrial and robotic systems.
people.name: Jürgen Schmidhuber
people.moniker: Scientific Director, Swiss AI Lab IDSIA

people.hook: Krithivasan runs the largest IT services company in India and one of the largest in the world, and in September 2026 put its name on the largest AI data centre campus the country has announced: a 1 gigawatt, 250-acre, Rs 70,000 crore project in Hyderabad through the TCS subsidiary HyperVault. He reached the top of TCS after thirty-four years inside it, most of them running the banking, financial services and insurance business that is the company's biggest vertical. His stated programme as chief executive has been to build what TCS calls the world's largest AI-ready workforce, and the Hyderabad campus is the infrastructure side of that same claim.
people.name: K. Krithivasan
people.moniker: CEO and Managing Director, Tata Consultancy Services

people.hook: Kaiming He earned a bachelor degree from Tsinghua University and a PhD in information engineering from the Chinese University of Hong Kong. He joined Microsoft Research Asia in 2011, where he authored Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition with Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun in 2015, introducing the residual connection that let networks scale past a thousand layers without degrading. In 2016 he moved to Facebook AI Research, where he co-created Mask R-CNN for instance segmentation. In 2024 he joined MIT as an Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science while continuing as a part-time Distinguished Scientist at Google DeepMind.
people.name: Kaiming He
people.moniker: Primary inventor of ResNet and Mask R-CNN

people.hook: Karen Simonyan studied at the University of Oxford, working in the Visual Geometry Group under Andrew Zisserman. In 2014 the pair published Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition, known as VGGNet, which showed that stacking small 3x3 convolutional filters into very deep networks of 16 to 19 layers produced strong image classification results. He joined DeepMind, where he worked on multimodal and generative systems including WaveNet and later large multimodal models. In 2022 he co-founded Inflection AI with Reid Hoffman and Mustafa Suleyman as chief scientist, and in 2024 moved to Microsoft as part of the team that formed Microsoft AI.
people.name: Karen Simonyan
people.moniker: Co-creator of VGGNet

people.hook: Karen Spärck Jones studied history and moral sciences at Girton College, Cambridge, then turned to natural language processing and information retrieval, joining the Cambridge Language Research Unit and later the Computer Laboratory at the University of Cambridge. In 1972 she published A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval, introducing inverse document frequency as a way to weight how informative a word is across a document collection. IDF became one half of TF-IDF, the weighting scheme that underpinned search engines for decades and remains a building block of modern text retrieval and vector search systems. She spent her career at Cambridge, served as president of the Association for Computational Linguistics, and was an outspoken advocate for women in computing.
people.name: Karen Spärck Jones
people.moniker: Inventor of inverse document frequency

people.hook: Dixon became Chancellor of North Carolina Central University in 2024 after leading Elizabeth City State University for over eight years, including as interim and then permanent Chancellor, and after six years overseeing academic and student affairs system-wide for the 17-campus University of North Carolina system. Her research has focused on college access and summer bridge programs.
people.name: Karrie G. Dixon
people.moniker: Chancellor, North Carolina Central University

people.hook: Shankel built her career in the operational and technical backbone of the automotive industry, general management, manufacturing processes, market expansion, before moving into the CTO seat at a commercial vehicle manufacturer and then founding her own technology company. Her PhD in organizational leadership combined with hands-on OEM manufacturing experience places her at the intersection of people-driven transformation and industrial technology adoption.
people.name: Kelleigh Shankel
people.moniker: CEO of Limelight Logic

people.hook: Kenneth Mark Colby was born in 1920 in Waterbury, Connecticut, and trained as a physician, graduating from Yale University in 1941 and Yale Medical School in 1943 before turning to psychoanalysis. In the early 1960s he moved to Stanford University's computer science department, where he began applying computational models to psychiatric theory. There he created PARRY, a natural language program that simulated the conversational patterns of a person with paranoid schizophrenia by weighting incoming statements as threatening or benign and responding with scripted defensive strategies. In 1972 PARRY and Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA were connected over the ARPANET at the International Conference on Computer Communications, producing one of the first recorded conversations between two artificial conversational agents. Colby later joined UCLA as a professor of psychiatry with a joint appointment in computer science, continued his research on computational models of mental illness, and died on April 20, 2001, at the age of 81.
people.name: Kenneth Colby
people.moniker: Psychiatrist who built PARRY

people.hook: Milchanowski built her career at the intersection of AI and financial crime, from model risk management at JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley to leading a global AI and quantum lab at EY that supported the U.S. National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence, before becoming BMO's first Chief AI and Quantum Officer and founding director of its applied AI institute.
people.name: Kristin Milchanowski
people.moniker: Chief AI and Quantum Officer at BMO Financial Group

people.hook: Kurt Godel was born on April 28, 1906, in Brno, then part of Austria-Hungary and now in the Czech Republic, and enrolled at the University of Vienna in 1923 to study mathematics after beginning in physics. In 1931 he published his incompleteness theorems, proving that any consistent formal system powerful enough to describe basic arithmetic contains true statements that cannot be proved within that system, and that such a system cannot prove its own consistency. The result answered a central question posed by David Hilbert's program to place all of mathematics on a complete and provable logical foundation, and it did so by showing that goal was unreachable. Godel first visited the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1933 and, after the Nazi annexation of Austria closed off his position at the University of Vienna, emigrated permanently to the United States in 1940. He became a full professor at the Institute for Advanced Study in 1953, worked there for the rest of his life alongside Albert Einstein and John von Neumann, and died on January 14, 1978, in Princeton, New Jersey.
people.name: Kurt Godel
people.moniker: Logician who proved the limits of formal systems

people.hook: Kyunghyun Cho earned a BSc in computer science from KAIST before completing an MSc and DSc in machine learning at Aalto University in Finland. During a postdoctoral fellowship with Yoshua Bengio at the Universite de Montreal, he co-authored Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation in 2014, which introduced the gated recurrent unit as a simpler alternative to the LSTM and helped establish the encoder-decoder framework used across neural machine translation. He joined the Courant Institute at New York University in 2015, became a research scientist at Facebook AI Research from 2017 to 2020, and returned to lead work at NYU, later co-heading the Global AI Frontier Lab with Yann LeCun and taking a professorship in health statistics.
people.name: Kyunghyun Cho
people.moniker: Co-inventor of the GRU and neural machine translation

people.hook: Morgan's career is a direct map of where AI governance is coming from in media and entertainment: she built operational legal structures for emerging digital platforms, streaming, apps, immersive venues, before the AI inflection point arrived, then moved into AI legal strategy at Amazon and NBCUniversal. The frameworks she builds now govern how a company the size of NBCU evaluates, procures, and deploys AI across its entire enterprise.
people.name: Lasherelle Morgan
people.moniker: SVP, Legal AI Innovation at NBCUniversal

people.hook: Leo Breiman earned a physics degree from Caltech in 1949, a master's degree in mathematics from Columbia in 1950, and a PhD from UC Berkeley in 1954, after which he taught probability theory at UCLA. He later resigned his tenured position to spend more than a decade as an independent statistical consultant, working on problems like traffic pattern and ozone level prediction, before joining the UC Berkeley Department of Statistics faculty in 1980. With Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees, published in 1984, and in 1996 he introduced Bagging, a method of averaging predictions across bootstrap samples to reduce variance. In 2001 he introduced Random Forests, an ensemble of randomized decision trees that became one of the most widely used machine learning algorithms, and published Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures, an influential essay on competing approaches to statistical inference. He died at his home in Berkeley, California, on July 5, 2005, following a prolonged illness.
people.name: Leo Breiman
people.moniker: Professor of Statistics, University of California, Berkeley

people.hook: Lisa Su has led AMD since October 2014, combining an electrical-engineering research background with semiconductor operations experience to turn the company from a distant also-ran into a primary supplier of AI accelerator hardware. Her MI300 and MI400 series GPUs gave large AI labs and cloud providers a credible second source of high-end accelerators alongside Nvidia. Su holds three degrees in electrical engineering from MIT and built her career through technical and general-management roles at Texas Instruments, IBM, and Freescale Semiconductor before joining AMD in 2012. She was named Time's CEO of the Year in 2024 and continues to set AMD's AI infrastructure roadmap, from CES keynotes to plans for trillion-parameter-scale training clusters.
people.name: Lisa Su
people.moniker: Chair and Chief Executive Officer, AMD

people.hook: Llion Jones grew up in Wales and earned a master's degree in advanced computer science from the University of Birmingham. He joined Google in 2012, first working as a software engineer on YouTube before moving into machine intelligence and natural language research around 2015. In 2017 he was one of eight Google researchers who co-authored Attention Is All You Need, the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture now underlying most large language models. He spent nearly twelve years at Google, then left in August 2023, citing frustration with internal bureaucracy and difficulty getting access to compute and data. He co-founded Sakana AI in Tokyo that year with fellow ex-Google researcher David Ha, taking the role of Chief Technology Officer and pursuing nature-inspired approaches to AI research as an alternative to simply building ever larger models.
people.name: Llion Jones
people.moniker: Co-founder and CTO, Sakana AI

people.hook: Lotfi Zadeh was born in Baku and later studied in Tehran before completing further degrees at MIT and Columbia University. He spent nine years on the electrical engineering faculty at Columbia before moving to the University of California, Berkeley in 1959, where he later chaired the Electrical Engineering Department from 1963 to 1968 and helped rename it the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences. In 1965 he published the paper Fuzzy Sets in the journal Information and Control, introducing a mathematical framework for representing categories that admit degrees of membership rather than strict true or false boundaries. That single paper launched fuzzy set theory and, later, fuzzy logic, which spread from control engineering into consumer electronics, decision analysis and approaches to reasoning under uncertainty in artificial intelligence. Zadeh remained a prolific researcher at Berkeley for the rest of his career, publishing more than two hundred papers and receiving numerous honors including the IEEE Medal of Honor and the Benjamin Franklin Medal.
people.name: Lotfi Zadeh
people.moniker: Founder of fuzzy set theory and fuzzy logic

people.hook: Lukasz Kaiser earned a master's degree from the University of Wroclaw in Poland and a PhD from RWTH Aachen University in Germany in 2008, working on logic and automata theory. He then spent time as a tenured researcher at Paris Diderot University before joining Google Brain in 2013. There he helped build the TensorFlow system and later co-created the Tensor2Tensor and Trax libraries used for sequence modeling research. In 2017 he co-authored Attention Is All You Need, contributing to the Transformer architecture that reshaped natural language processing. He later moved to OpenAI, where he worked as a research scientist and was credited as the long context lead on the GPT-4 project, helping extend how much text the model could take into account at once.
people.name: Lukasz Kaiser
people.moniker: Research scientist, OpenAI, and co-author of the Transformer

people.hook: Beck has spent over 17 years inside Daimler's IT organisation, running IT for Daimler Trucks Asia and Mitsubishi Fuso from Tokyo before becoming CIO of Daimler Truck North America in 2018, where he also now heads IT for autonomous driving. He speaks German, English, French, and Spanish.
people.name: Lutz Beck
people.moniker: CIO, Daimler Truck North America

people.hook: Marc Raibert is a roboticist known as the founder of Boston Dynamics. He held research and faculty positions at Carnegie Mellon University and MIT, where he ran the MIT Leg Lab studying dynamic, legged locomotion in robots. In 1992 he spun the lab's work out of MIT to found Boston Dynamics, joined soon after by Robert Playter. Under his leadership the company built a series of dynamically balancing robots, including BigDog, Cheetah, Atlas, and Spot, that became widely recognized demonstrations of legged robotics. Boston Dynamics passed through ownership by Google's X division, SoftBank Group, and Hyundai Motor Company over the following decades, and Raibert stepped back from the CEO role while remaining involved with the company. He now serves as Executive Director of the Robotics and AI Institute, which he leads from offices in Cambridge, Massachusetts and Zurich, Switzerland.
people.name: Marc Raibert
people.moniker: Robotics pioneer, founder of Boston Dynamics

people.hook: Margaret Mitchell is an AI researcher whose work focuses on documentation and transparency practices meant to make machine learning systems more accountable. Working across natural language processing and computer vision, she has held research roles at Microsoft Research, Google, and now Hugging Face. In 2018 she was the lead author of Model Cards for Model Reporting, a paper written with a team of Google and academic researchers, including Timnit Gebru, that proposed short standardized documents to accompany released machine learning models describing how they perform across different conditions and demographic groups. The model card format she helped design was later adopted widely across the AI industry. At Hugging Face she works on the company's Society and Ethics research efforts and contributes to open research initiatives such as the BigScience and BigCode workshops. Her research continues to center on practical tools, such as model documentation and bias evaluation methods, that let developers and the public better understand what a given AI system does and does not do well.
people.name: Margaret Mitchell
people.moniker: AI ethics researcher and co-creator of Model Cards

people.hook: Mark Chen has been at OpenAI since 2018, moving from quantitative trading into leading some of the company's most visible research programs. He co-led the team that built DALL-E, directed the vision work that gave GPT-4 its multimodal capabilities, and oversaw Codex, the model behind GitHub Copilot. In March 2025 OpenAI named him Chief Research Officer, a role focused on integrating research and product development so new capabilities move into deployment faster. He also coaches the USA Computing Olympiad team, a pastime that tracks with his own path through competitive mathematics and computer science at MIT.
people.name: Mark Chen
people.moniker: Chief Research Officer, OpenAI

people.hook: Marvin Minsky earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Harvard in 1950 and a PhD in mathematics from Princeton in 1954, having already built SNARC, an early neural network learning machine, as a student in 1951. In 1955 he joined John McCarthy, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon in writing the proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, and in 1959 he co-founded what became the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with McCarthy, directing it for many years. In 1969, with Seymour Papert, Minsky published Perceptrons, a rigorous mathematical analysis of the capabilities and limits of a simple class of neural networks that influenced the direction of AI research for years afterward. He later developed frame theory as a way of representing knowledge in AI systems, and in 1985 published Society of Mind, arguing that intelligence emerges from the interaction of many simple, specialized processes rather than any single mechanism. Minsky received the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 1969 for his central role in creating, shaping and advancing the field of artificial intelligence.
people.name: Marvin Minsky
people.moniker: Co-founded the MIT AI Lab and shaped decades of artificial intelligence research

people.hook: Matei Zaharia grew up partly in Toronto and earned an undergraduate degree from the University of Waterloo before pursuing a PhD in computer science at UC Berkeley's AMPLab. There, starting in 2009, he created Apache Spark, an in-memory cluster computing engine that grew into one of the most widely used frameworks for large-scale data processing, and co-created the cluster manager Apache Mesos. After completing his PhD in 2013, he co-founded Databricks with Ion Stoica and other Berkeley colleagues to commercialize Spark, taking on the role of Chief Technology Officer. He held a faculty position at MIT CSAIL before moving to Stanford University, where he is now an associate professor of computer science co-directing research on data and AI systems. At Databricks he has also helped build MLflow and Delta Lake, and his more recent research examines combining large language models with external data sources.
people.name: Matei Zaharia
people.moniker: Creator of Apache Spark, co-founder and CTO of Databricks

people.hook: Max Welling earned his PhD in 1998 at Utrecht University under Nobel laureate physicist Gerard t Hooft before moving into machine learning through postdoctoral positions at Caltech, University College London and the University of Toronto. In 2013 he and Diederik Kingma published Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, introducing the variational autoencoder and a reparameterization trick that made it possible to train deep generative latent-variable models with backpropagation. He became a professor at the University of Amsterdam, where he directs the Amsterdam Machine Learning Lab, and in 2016 he and Thomas Kipf published Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks, extending convolutional architectures to graph-structured data. He has also held research leadership roles at Microsoft Research and Qualcomm.
people.name: Max Welling
people.moniker: Co-inventor of the variational autoencoder and graph convolutional network

people.hook: Wallace serves as President and CEO of Huston-Tillotson University in Austin, Texas, a historically Black university.
people.name: Melva Wallace
people.moniker: President and CEO, Huston-Tillotson University

people.hook: Michael I. Jordan earned a master's degree in mathematics from Arizona State University and a PhD in cognitive science from the University of California, San Diego in 1985. He joined the faculty of MIT in 1988, before moving to the University of California, Berkeley in 1998. At Berkeley he holds the Pehong Chen Distinguished Professorship jointly in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Department of Statistics. His research connects statistics, optimization and computer science, with major contributions to probabilistic graphical models, variational inference and Bayesian nonparametric methods that shaped how modern machine learning systems reason under uncertainty. He has also been an outspoken voice pushing back on hype around artificial general intelligence, arguing in his widely read 2018 essay that the field needs a genuine engineering discipline built around real world human centered systems rather than science fiction narratives about human imitative AI.
people.name: Michael I. Jordan
people.moniker: Pehong Chen Distinguished Professor, UC Berkeley

people.hook: Michael J. Jones earned his PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1997. Working with Paul Viola, he co-developed the Viola-Jones object detection framework, published as Rapid Object Detection using a Boosted Cascade of Simple Features in 2001, which combined Haar-like features, an integral image representation and a cascade of boosted classifiers to make real-time face detection possible on ordinary hardware for the first time. The pair extended the work into Robust Real-Time Face Detection in 2004. Jones continued his career at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, where he became a Distinguished Research Scientist working on computer vision, machine learning and data analytics, including detection and analysis of people in images and video.
people.name: Michael Jones
people.moniker: Co-inventor of the Viola-Jones object detection framework

people.hook: Tripathi has spent his career on the unglamorous but consequential work of making health data actually move between systems, first from the policy side as the U.S. government's top health IT official, and now from inside a leading hospital system, applying that same interoperability and governance discipline to how AI gets deployed in clinical care.
people.name: Micky Tripathi
people.moniker: Federal Architect of Health AI Policy

people.hook: Miles Brundage is an AI policy researcher who spent six years at OpenAI working on how the world should prepare for increasingly capable AI systems. He holds a BA in political science from George Washington University and a PhD in the Human and Social Dimensions of Science and Technology from Arizona State University, completed in 2019, with earlier stints at ARPA-E and the Institute for Human and Machine Cognition. From 2016 to 2018 he was a research fellow at Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute before joining OpenAI in 2018 as a research scientist on its policy team. Over six years there he rose to head of policy research and then senior advisor for AGI readiness, leading the company's external red-teaming program and developing its first system cards for documenting model capabilities. He left OpenAI in October 2024, saying he wanted to influence AI's development from outside industry, and went on to found AVERI, a nonprofit focused on independent AI policy research, while advising organizations including the Institute for Progress, CNAS, Epoch AI and RAND.
people.name: Miles Brundage
people.moniker: AI policy researcher, former OpenAI senior advisor for AGI readiness

people.hook: Mustafa Suleyman was born in London in 1984 and studied at the University of Oxford. In 2010 he co-founded DeepMind, an artificial intelligence research lab that Google acquired in 2014, where he went on to lead applied AI and policy work. After leaving Google in 2019 and a period as a venture partner at Greylock, he co-founded Inflection AI in March 2022 with Reid Hoffman and Karen Simonyan, building the Pi personal assistant and the Inflection-2.5 model. In 2023 he published The Coming Wave, a book arguing that AI and synthetic biology pose a containment problem for governments and societies. In March 2024 he joined Microsoft as CEO of Microsoft AI, leading the Copilot consumer AI effort, and he has continued to write and speak about what he calls building humanist superintelligence.
people.name: Mustafa Suleyman
people.moniker: CEO, Microsoft AI

people.hook: Nick Bostrom is a Swedish philosopher who has shaped how both academics and the public think about the long term risks and possibilities of advanced technology. He trained across physics, computational neuroscience, and philosophy at the universities of Gothenburg, Stockholm, and King's College London, and completed a PhD in philosophy at the London School of Economics in 2000. In 2002 he published the paper Existential Risks, which introduced a systematic taxonomy of the ways humanity's long term potential could be destroyed or permanently curtailed. In 2005 he founded and directed the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University, building it from three researchers into a center that helped incubate the fields of AI safety and effective altruism before it closed in 2024. His 2014 book Superintelligence, Paths, Dangers, Strategies became a New York Times bestseller and is widely credited with moving concerns about advanced AI from niche discussion into mainstream academic and public debate. He continues this work as founder of the Macrostrategy Research Initiative, and published the book Deep Utopia in 2024.
people.name: Nick Bostrom
people.moniker: Philosopher of existential risk and superintelligence

people.hook: Nick Frosst studied computer science and cognitive science at the University of Toronto, working with researchers including John Tsotsos, Sanja Fidler and Jimmy Ba. He became the first employee of Geoffrey Hinton's Google Brain lab in Toronto, where he spent three years researching capsule networks, adversarial examples and model explainability. During that time he co-authored "Dynamic Routing Between Capsules" with Sara Sabour and Geoffrey Hinton, a widely cited paper proposing an alternative to standard convolutional pooling. In 2019 he left Google to co-found Cohere with Aidan Gomez and Ivan Zhang, building an enterprise-focused large language model company. Alongside his machine learning career, Frosst is also an active musician.
people.name: Nick Frosst
people.moniker: Co-founder of Cohere, capsule networks researcher

people.hook: Niki Parmar earned a bachelor's degree in information technology from the Pune Institute of Computer Technology in India, then a master's degree in computer science from the University of Southern California. She joined Google in 2015 as an engineer and research scientist, working on end to end deep learning systems for natural language processing. In 2017, reportedly the youngest member of her team and the only one without a PhD, she co-authored Attention Is All You Need, the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture. She spent close to seven years at Google before co-founding Adept AI Labs in 2022 as Chief Technology Officer, building enterprise workflow automation tools, and then co-founding Essential AI in 2023 to build full stack AI products for automating data processing, with backing from Google and Nvidia. She has since also worked as a member of technical staff at Anthropic on reliable and interpretable AI systems.
people.name: Niki Parmar
people.moniker: Co-founder, Essential AI

people.hook: Nils Nilsson earned his PhD in electrical engineering from Stanford in 1958, then served in the United States Air Force before joining SRI International, where he spent 23 years building foundational tools for artificial intelligence. At SRI he co-invented the A* search algorithm and the STRIPS automated planning system, and co-directed Shakey, one of the first mobile robots able to perceive its surroundings, plan, and act. He returned to Stanford in 1985 and chaired its Computer Science Department until 1990, later becoming the Kumagai Professor of Engineering, Emeritus. Nilsson wrote nine books on artificial intelligence, including the 2010 history The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, and served as president of AAAI. He died in 2019 in Medford, Oregon, at age 86.
people.name: Nils Nilsson
people.moniker: AI pioneer, Stanford University and SRI International

people.hook: Noam Shazeer joined Google in 2000, where he first worked on improving the search engine's spelling correction and helped develop the PHIL algorithm that became central to Google AdSense. Over the next two decades he moved into deep learning, co-authoring a paper on sparsely gated mixture of experts models in 2016 and then, in 2017, co-authoring Attention Is All You Need, where he designed the multi-head attention mechanism at the core of the Transformer. He went on to create Mesh-TensorFlow in 2018 for training large Transformers across many machines, co-authored the T5 model in 2019, and contributed to Google's LaMDA dialogue system. In 2021 he left Google to co-found Character.AI with Daniel De Freitas, serving as its CEO and building one of the first consumer chatbots built on Transformer technology. In August 2024 he returned to Google as part of a licensing deal with Character.AI, rejoining Google DeepMind's research team, and later co-led development of the Gemini model as Vice President of Engineering before departing for OpenAI in June 2026.
people.name: Noam Shazeer
people.moniker: AI researcher, OpenAI

people.hook: Arbaugh went from a diving accident that left him paralyzed to becoming, at 29, the first person on Earth to use a brain implant to control a computer in daily life, turning his own recovery into the most closely watched real-world test of whether brain-computer interfaces can restore independence.
people.name: Noland Arbaugh
people.moniker: The World's First Neuralink Patient

people.hook: Norbert Wiener was a mathematical prodigy who earned a bachelor's degree from Tufts College at 14 and a PhD in philosophy from Harvard at 19, then studied with Bertrand Russell in Cambridge and David Hilbert in Gottingen. He joined MIT's Department of Mathematics in 1919 and remained there for 45 years, doing foundational work in stochastic processes, harmonic analysis, and what became known as the Wiener process. During the Second World War he worked on statistical prediction methods for anti-aircraft fire control, research that pushed him toward a broader theory of control and communication. In 1948 he published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, founding the field of cybernetics and giving later computing and AI research a vocabulary for feedback loops. His 1950 book The Human Use of Human Beings extended these ideas to society, warning early about the social effects of automation. He became an MIT Institute Professor in 1959 and died in 1964 while traveling in Stockholm, Sweden.
people.name: Norbert Wiener
people.moniker: Founder of cybernetics, MIT

people.hook: Norman Jouppi earned a master's degree in electrical engineering from Northwestern University in 1980 and a PhD in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1984, where he was one of the principal architects of the MIPS microprocessor. He spent much of his early career at Digital Equipment Corporation's Western Research Laboratory researching computer memory systems, microprocessor architecture and graphics accelerators, work that carried through DEC's acquisition by Compaq and Compaq's later acquisition by Hewlett-Packard, where he was named an HP Senior Fellow in 2010. He joined Google in the early 2010s and became technical lead for the company's Tensor Processing Units from their inception, with the first generation deployed in Google datacenters starting in 2015. He was lead author of "In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit," published at ISCA in 2017, which documented the chip's real-world performance and became one of the most cited papers in computer architecture. He now holds the title of Vice President and Engineering Fellow at Google, continuing to lead AI infrastructure and TPU development.
people.name: Norman Jouppi
people.moniker: Chief architect of Google's Tensor Processing Unit

people.hook: Oriol Vinyals was born in Sabadell, Spain, in 1983 and trained as both a mathematician and a telecommunications engineer at the Polytechnic University of Catalonia before completing graduate work at Carnegie Mellon and UC San Diego. He earned a PhD in electrical engineering and computer sciences from UC Berkeley in 2013, working on machine learning during internships at Google and Microsoft Research. He joined Google Brain the same year and helped develop sequence to sequence learning, a technique that let a single neural network translate and generate text without hand built rules. In 2016 he moved to Google DeepMind in London, where he became Vice President of Research and led the deep learning team behind AlphaStar, the system that beat professional StarCraft II players, and served as a technical co-lead on the Gemini model family. His sequence learning work also underpins AlphaFold, the protein structure system that won two of his DeepMind colleagues the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
people.name: Oriol Vinyals
people.moniker: VP of Research, Google DeepMind

people.hook: Gelsinger's career traces the arc of modern computing hardware itself: chief architect of a landmark Intel processor in his twenties, the company's first CTO, then, decades later, recalled as CEO to fight for American chip manufacturing leadership just as AI's compute demands made semiconductors a national priority.
people.name: Pat Gelsinger
people.moniker: Engineer Who Led Intel's Turnaround Attempt

people.hook: Patrick Esser studied computer vision at the IWR institute of Heidelberg University, working in Björn Ommer's Computer Vision group alongside Robin Rombach. In 2020 the pair co-authored VQGAN, published as Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis, which combined a convolutional vector quantized autoencoder with a transformer to generate high resolution images. The following year he co-authored High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models with Rombach, Andreas Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz and Ommer, the paper that introduced latent diffusion and became the technical basis for Stable Diffusion. Esser and several of his CompVis colleagues later worked at Stability AI before leaving in 2024 to co-found Black Forest Labs with Rombach and Blattmann, an independent lab based in Freiburg, Germany, focused on generative visual models. The new company released its FLUX family of image generation models the same year it launched.
people.name: Patrick Esser
people.moniker: Co-founder, Black Forest Labs

people.hook: Paul Christiano holds a PhD in statistical learning theory from UC Berkeley. While working on the alignment team at OpenAI, he was a co-author and principal architect of the 2017 paper Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences, which introduced the technique now known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, using human comparisons between possible outputs to train reinforcement learning systems. That approach was later adapted to fine-tune large language models and became a standard part of how systems like ChatGPT are trained to follow instructions and match human judgment. In 2021 he left OpenAI to found the Alignment Research Center (ARC), a nonprofit that develops theoretical and empirical methods for understanding and evaluating advanced AI systems, including work on eliciting latent knowledge from neural networks. He was named to the Time 100 Most Influential People in AI in 2023, and in 2024 he began advising the U.S. government's AI safety evaluation work through what is now NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation.
people.name: Paul Christiano
people.moniker: Founder, Alignment Research Center

people.hook: Paul Scharre is a former Army Ranger turned defense policy analyst who leads work on autonomous weapons and AI strategy at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS). He served as a special operations reconnaissance team leader in the Army's 3rd Ranger Battalion, deploying multiple times to Iraq and Afghanistan, before moving into the Office of the Secretary of Defense. There he directed the working group that wrote DoD Directive 3000.09, the Pentagon's foundational policy on autonomy in weapons systems, and contributed to the 2010 Quadrennial Defense Review and the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance. He holds a PhD in war studies from King's College London and a master's and bachelor's from Washington University in St. Louis. At CNAS he wrote Army of None, a 2018 book on autonomous weapons that won the William E. Colby Award and was named one of Bill Gates' top five books of the year, and Four Battlegrounds, a 2023 book on the global contest for AI power that led to his inclusion on TIME's inaugural TIME100/AI list.
people.name: Paul Scharre
people.moniker: Executive Vice President, Center for a New American Security

people.hook: Paul Viola was born in New York City on October 22, 1966, and studied at MIT, earning a PhD in 1995 with a thesis on alignment by maximization of mutual information under advisors Christopher Atkeson and Tomas Lozano-Perez.
